title: Probability and Distributions
lines: Probability questions in USAT are short but unforgiving: one miscounted outcome and the answer is wrong. Expect counting with permutations and combinations, dice, coins and cards, the addition and multiplication laws, conditional probability, expectation of a random variable, and the binomial, Poisson and normal distributions at HSSC Part II level.
## Counting
- Multiplication principle: if one task can be done in m ways and another in n ways, both can be done in m × n ways.
- Permutations (order matters): ⁿPᵣ = n! ÷ (n − r)!. Combinations (order does not matter): ⁿCᵣ = n! ÷ [r!(n − r)!].
- n objects with p alike: n! ÷ p!. n people round a table: (n − 1)!.
- ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ, so ¹⁰C₈ = ¹⁰C₂ = 45.
! President and secretary are different posts, so use ⁿPᵣ. A committee has no posts, so use ⁿCᵣ.
## Basic probability
For equally likely outcomes, P(A) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, and 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1. The complement rule is P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
| Experiment | Outcomes | Useful facts
| One die | 6 | P(any one face) = 1/6
| Two dice | 36 | total 7 has 6 ways; doubles have 6 ways
| n coins | 2ⁿ | three coins give 8 outcomes
| Pack of cards | 52 | 4 suits of 13; 26 red; 4 kings; 12 face cards
## Laws of probability
- Addition law: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For mutually exclusive events P(A ∩ B) = 0.
- Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B).
- Multiplication law: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B | A); for independent events P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
- Total probability and Bayes: if B₁, B₂ split the sample space, P(A) = ΣP(Bᵢ)P(A | Bᵢ) and P(B₁ | A) = P(B₁)P(A | B₁) ÷ P(A).
> Example 1. A card is drawn from 52. P(red or king)?
> 26/52 + 4/52 − 2/52 = 28/52 = 7/13. The two red kings must not be counted twice.
> Example 2. A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls; two are drawn without replacement. P(both red)?
> 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15. With replacement it would be (4/10)² = 4/25.
! Mutually exclusive is not the same as independent. Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities can never be independent.
## Random variables and expectation
A discrete random variable X has a list of values with probabilities that add to 1.
- E(X) = Σx·P(x); Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
- E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X).
## Binomial distribution
Use it for a fixed number n of independent trials, each with two outcomes and the same chance p of success (q = 1 − p).
- P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ, r = 0, 1, …, n.
- Mean = np; variance = npq, which is always less than the mean. Symmetrical when p = ½.
> Example 4. Mean 6 and variance 4.2: q = 4.2 ÷ 6 = 0.7, p = 0.3, n = 6 ÷ 0.3 = 20.
## Poisson distribution

For counts of rare events with many chances (calls per minute, misprints per page): P(X = r) = e⁻ᵐ mʳ ÷ r!. Mean = variance = m. It approximates the binomial when n is large and p small, with m = np. USAT will give you the value of e⁻ᵐ when needed.
## Normal distribution
- Bell-shaped, symmetrical about μ; mean = median = mode; total area 1; points of inflection at μ ± σ.
- Standardise with z = (x − μ) ÷ σ; Z has mean 0 and variance 1.
| Interval | Area
| μ ± 1σ | about 68 %
| μ ± 2σ | about 95 %
| μ ± 3σ | about 99.7 %
! For one tail, halve what is left outside: above μ + 2σ is about (100 − 95) ÷ 2 = 2.5 %.
## Quick check
- How many arrangements does the word KARACHI have? (Two A's.)
- P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, independent. Find P(A ∪ B).
- A binomial has n = 25, p = 0.2. Find its mean and S.D.
- Marks have μ = 50, σ = 5. About what share score below 40?
